newsitem.title: UK: Mark rangebound in Europe, ignores EMU comments.
newsitem.headline: Mark rangebound in Europe, ignores EMU comments.

text.p: The mark was little changed on its European crosses as the market digested various comments concerning European monetary union, while it held on to gains against the Swedish crown.
Markets would be looking to U.S. March industrial production data due out at 1315 GMT to give the European currencies direction, analysts said.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said Germany still had a chance to meet the three percent EMU budget deficit target, and dismissed speculation about relaxed budget deficit-to-GDP criteria, saying "3.0 is 3.0."

"Anything that suggests that there won't be a fudge may provide a lift, but I think the market wants to see some numbers coming in first to judge whether the EMU qualification interpretation will be loose or not," Bank America chief European economist Jeremy Hawkins said.
The EMU qualification criteria should be "applied stringently", Waigel said.
The Bundesbank said in its April monthly report it saw no indication that investors were pulling out of mark investments in response to EMU uncertainty.
"There was no real reaction (in the mark crosses) to the Bundesbank report," said Michael Lewis, senior international economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Meanwhile, Italian business daily Il Sole 24 Ore cited sources in Bonn saying a deal was taking shape between France and Germany to keep Spain and Italy out of the first wave of EMU.

Senior European officials denied the report, with Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi saying there were no such "secret deals" and a French Finance Ministry official saying such a deal was "completely absurd".
Mark/lira was trading at 984.80/5.10 at 1205 GMT compared with 983.35/65 late on Tuesday.
Italian February producer data due later on Wednesday is forecast to rise by 0.8 percent year-on-year.
Italy's Ciampi and Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco are meeting to detail state account reforms, and reforms to fiscal and public administration.
Mark/peseta remained little changed at 84.28/4.31 against 84.22/23 late on Tuesday.
The mark held on to gains against the Swedish crown in the wake of Sweden's expansionary budget announcement on Tuesday, though it was off fresh five-week highs.

"If you add yesterday's budget disappointment to current political risk in Sweden and the fact that Sweden will remain outside EMU's first wave, you can't expect the Swedish crown to outperform," First Chicago international economist Teis Knuthsen said.
Sweden's spring budget announcement forecast a balanced budget for 1998 and not a surplus as previously forecast.
First Chicago's Knuthsen said this meant an increased risk of further spending packages before Sweden's 1998 general election.
The Swedish government also announced it would spend an extra 20 billion crowns by the end of 1998 on education and lowering unemployment.
Mark/Swedish crown was trading at 4.4520/50 against 4.4435/65 late on Tuesday.
Mark/Swiss franc was off a four-month low of 84.75 hit overnight, trading at 84.98/01 compared with 84.79/82 late on Tuesday.

"It's a bit of a correction (after its drop). With the Dow up the past couple of days and (strength in) U.S. asset markets spilling over into other asset markets, the Swiss franc will come under pressure," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank.
--Simon Gardner, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 6762
